strengths: First systematic theoretical treatment of false-positive cluster/outlier artifacts in t-SNE, filling an explicitly identified gap in prior work (which focused on true-positive guarantees for well-separated inputs).

Clean and rigorous mathematical development: the identification of t-SNE's invariance to both multiplicative and additive rescaling of squared interpoint distances (via a clever application of the Schoenberg embedding theorem) is a novel and illuminating structural insight that unifies the main results.

Results are stated generally and shown to hold across multiple standard cluster-validity indices (silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Dunn), strengthening the claim that the phenomenon is not an artifact of a particular metric.

Strong complementary empirical validation on both synthetic and real-world datasets (single-cell PBMC genomics, credit-card fraud, BBC news RoBERTa embeddings), showing the theoretical failure modes (impostor datasets, poison-point attacks, outlier masking) are practically realizable, not just adversarial curiosities.
The outlier suppression result (Theorem 8) gives a clean, input-agnostic bound and is supported by a compelling contrast with PCA on real fraud-detection data.
Practical relevance is well-articulated: implications for downstream scientific interpretation (e.g., genomics, anomaly/fraud detection) are clearly discussed.
Code availability supports reproducibility, and proofs are relegated to a thorough appendix, keeping the main text readable.
weaknesses: The main constructive theorems (3, 5, 6) rely on the very permissive notion of 'stationary point' (any critical point of the KL objective), not the actual output of gradient descent with early exaggeration as run in practice; it is not fully established that the constructed adversarial/impostor datasets are reachable by standard t-SNE optimization procedures (initialization + early exaggeration + gradient descent), which somewhat weakens the practical bite of the pure existence results, even though the empirical sections partially address this gap.

The dimensionality assumption D = n-1 used throughout the theory (needed for the Schoenberg-embedding argument) is quite restrictive relative to typical real-world datasets where D is fixed and much smaller than n; the paper's 'without loss of generality' framing could be misleading and deserves more discussion of how the results degrade or transfer to lower-dimensional, structured inputs.

The theoretical outlier bound (α ≤ 3, Theorem 8) is far looser than what is empirically observed (α rarely exceeds 0.2 in practice); the gap between the theoretical worst case and empirical typical case is not discussed, leaving the practical tightness of the bound unclear.

The paper does not examine whether the identified pathologies (additive invariance, affinity asymmetry) are unique to t-SNE or are shared by related methods (e.g., UMAP), which would help contextualize the significance and generality of the findings.

Limited actionable guidance for practitioners: the discussion section raises the important open question but offers little concrete advice on how to detect or mitigate these failure modes in routine data-analysis workflows.

Some of the density/notational complexity (e.g., the interplay of σ*, perplexity, Definition 1) may hinder accessibility to the broader ML/data-visualization audience who use t-SNE without deep familiarity with its optimization theory.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely question—whether t-SNE visualizations can be trusted to reflect true cluster/outlier structure—which has real consequences in fields like single-cell genomics.

Provides genuine theoretical contributions (Theorems 3, 5, 8) with full proofs, identifying a previously under-formalized property of t-SNE: invariance of the input affinity matrix to additive shifts in squared interpoint distances, which explains several counter-intuitive behaviors.

Combines theory with concrete constructive demonstrations (impostor dataset algorithm, poison-point attacks, α-outlier constructions) and validates the phenomena on both synthetic and real-world datasets (PBMC3k, BBC News, credit-card fraud).
Results are shown to generalize across multiple clustering indices (silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Dunn index) rather than being tied to one metric.
Clear contrast with PCA baseline helps contextualize the severity of t-SNE's failure modes.
Related work section reasonably situates the paper among prior theoretical guarantees (Arora et al., Linderman & Steinerberger) and empirical criticisms (Yang et al., Chari & Pachter).
weaknesses: The theoretical framework (Definition 1) considers the set of ALL stationary points of the t-SNE objective, not the specific output reached by the standard algorithm (early exaggeration + gradient descent + typical initialization). While the empirical sections partly bridge this gap, the core theorems (existence of adversarial stationary configurations) do not strictly guarantee that practical t-SNE runs would actually converge to these pathological embeddings from typical initializations, leaving a gap between the formal claims and practical relevance.

The central technical mechanism—that input affinities are invariant to additive shifts because per-point bandwidths are calibrated to match a fixed perplexity/entropy target—is a fairly direct consequence of the known local-bandwidth normalization in t-SNE and may be seen as a relatively incremental formalization of an intuition already informally understood in the community (e.g., via Wattenberg et al.-style guidance and concentration-of-measure critiques), rather than a deeply surprising new mechanism.

The claimed novelty ("first work which theoretically analyzes some of the key limitations of t-SNE" in terms of false positives) is not fully reconciled with contemporaneous related work (Snoeck et al. 2025) which is only briefly distinguished in one sentence; overlap in scope/insight is not carefully delineated.

Real-world empirical validation is somewhat narrow (essentially three datasets: PBMC3k, BBC News, and a credit-card fraud subset), without broader coverage across domains, t-SNE hyperparameter settings (perplexity, learning rate, initialization schemes), or comparison to other embedding methods such as UMAP, despite UMAP being mentioned as a related technique subject to similar scrutiny.

The outlier bound in Theorem 8 (α ≤ ~3) is an asymptotic worst-case bound; the paper does not carefully characterize how tight or representative this bound is for realistic data distributions, nor does it explore how the bound depends on n or perplexity in more depth beyond the asymptotic statement.

The adversarial constructions (impostor datasets, poison points) require deliberately engineered or extreme configurations; the paper offers limited discussion of how frequently such conditions arise 'naturally' in real datasets beyond the illustrative examples, somewhat limiting the generality of the practical takeaway.
Presentation of some proofs (e.g., Corollary 4/10/12 combined proof) is dense and could benefit from more intuition-building for a broader audience.

strengths: Addresses an important and previously understudied gap in t-SNE theory: while prior work (Arora et al. 2018, Linderman & Steinerberger 2019) established that clustered inputs yield clustered outputs (true positives), this paper is the first to rigorously study the converse failure mode -- false positives/negatives, i.e., what can (and cannot) be inferred about the input from the t-SNE output.

The key technical insight -- that t-SNE is invariant not just to multiplicative but also additive rescaling of squared interpoint distances -- is elegant, non-obvious, and rigorously proved via a clean application of Schoenberg's embeddability theorem. This single observation is leveraged effectively to derive multiple strong results (Theorem 3, Corollary 4, Theorem 5, Lemma 6).

Results are shown to hold uniformly across multiple standard cluster-quality metrics (silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Dunn index), which strengthens the generality and robustness of the cluster-misrepresentation claims rather than relying on a single, possibly metric-specific artifact.

Theorem 8 provides a concrete, interpretable, input-agnostic bound (roughly α ≤ 3) showing t-SNE fundamentally cannot depict extreme outliers, contrasted clearly and convincingly against PCA both theoretically and empirically.

Strong, diverse empirical validation spanning synthetic constructions (regular simplices, Gaussian mixtures) and real-world datasets (PBMC3k single-cell genomics, credit card fraud detection, BBC news embeddings), directly tying the abstract theoretical mechanisms (additive invariance, affinity asymmetry) to practically observable and important failure modes (e.g., single poison-point attacks destroying visible cluster structure).

The adversarial "poison point" construction is a compelling, practically relevant demonstration that a single injected point can collapse an otherwise clean two-cluster visualization, illustrating real risk for downstream scientific interpretation.
Clear exposition; proofs are detailed, mostly self-contained, and placed in a well-organized appendix; code and reproducibility artifacts are referenced.
weaknesses: The main results establish existence of adversarial/impostor datasets, which is a worst-case style guarantee; although the paper supplements this with real-data experiments, it remains somewhat unclear how prevalent or likely these failure modes are for "typical" real-world data encountered in practice versus deliberately constructed or adversarial inputs.

The theory covers all stationary points of the t-SNE objective (Definition 1), not specifically the particular local minima that practical gradient-descent-with-early-exaggeration implementations converge to; it would strengthen the paper to discuss/empirically verify whether the constructed impostor/adversarial configurations are actually reachable by standard t-SNE optimization routines with typical initializations, rather than being merely stationary in principle.

PCA is used as essentially the sole baseline for contrast in the outlier and poison-point experiments; given that the related work section discusses UMAP and other embedding techniques, including at least one additional modern nonlinear method (e.g., UMAP) as a baseline would better contextualize how unique this failure mode is to t-SNE versus dimensionality reduction broadly (the cited Snoeck et al. 2025 result suggests it may be more general).

The paper offers limited practical guidance or mitigation strategies for practitioners beyond general caution; given the stated motivation (downstream scientific consequences), some discussion of diagnostic tools or safeguards would increase the paper's practical impact.

The geometric outlier definition (linear separability with margin relative to bulk diameter) is reasonable but specific; it is not discussed how this compares to more standard statistical/distance-based outlier notions, which may affect the generality of the outlier-misrepresentation claims.

strengths: Addresses a clear and important gap in the literature: while prior theory (Arora et al. 2018, Linderman & Steinerberger 2019) established when t-SNE reliably reveals true cluster structure, this paper is the first to rigorously characterize when and why t-SNE outputs can be misleading (false positives/negatives, outlier suppression).

The core theoretical insight - that t-SNE input affinities are invariant under additive shifts (and multiplicative scaling) of squared interpoint distances - is elegant, non-obvious, and used cleanly to derive several strong impossibility results (Theorem 3, Corollary 4, Theorem 5, Lemma 6).

Results are shown to generalize across multiple standard cluster-validity indices (silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Dunn), strengthening the claim that the phenomenon is not an artifact of a particular metric choice.

The outlier misrepresentation result (Theorem 9) gives an input-agnostic, dimension-independent bound on the outlier number depictable by any stationary t-SNE embedding, which is a strong and surprising structural result, and its proof via a careful gradient/stationarity argument is technically solid.

Extensive and well-designed empirical validation on both synthetic constructions and real datasets (PBMC3k single-cell genomics, credit card fraud detection, BBC news RoBERTa embeddings) that closely tracks the theory and makes the results concrete and convincing to practitioners.

Practical contribution of a simple, cheap single-point 'poison point' adversarial attack that can dramatically distort t-SNE visualizations, illustrating real-world exploitability of the theoretical vulnerability.

Good positioning relative to related work, including a thoughtful discussion of concurrent work (Snoeck et al.) and comparisons to UMAP/PCA showing the phenomena are not universal but relatively t-SNE-specific in the case of poison points.
Comprehensive appendix with full proofs, additional experiments (PCA pre-processing effects, additional dimension scalings, UMAP comparisons) that supports reproducibility and robustness of claims.
weaknesses: The adversarial constructions (impostor datasets, poison points, near-simplex perturbations) rely on very specific and somewhat contrived high-dimensional configurations (e.g., D = n-1 regular-simplex-like geometry); the paper would benefit from more discussion of how often such configurations arise 'naturally' versus needing deliberate adversarial construction, beyond the illustrative real-data examples.

The paper is purely diagnostic: it does not propose or evaluate any mitigation, robustified variant of t-SNE, or diagnostic tool that practitioners could use to guard against the identified failure modes, which somewhat limits its practical impact beyond a cautionary message.

The bound in Theorem 9 (α ≤ 3.266) is not shown to be tight, and there is little discussion of how loose this worst-case bound might be relative to typical behavior, or what happens with more outliers/structure - the empirical section suggests real behavior is much worse (α seldom exceeds 0.2), leaving a fairly large gap between theory and practice that isn't explained.
The GitHub code repository link appears to be omitted/blank in the submission ('available on Github at' is left incomplete), which is a reproducibility concern.

Given that a companion/contemporaneous work (Arora et al., Linderman & Steinerberger) already characterizes the 'positive' regime, and Yang et al. (2021)/Chari & Pachter (2023) already provide strong empirical evidence of similar failure modes, part of the paper's contribution is formalizing known empirical intuitions rather than uncovering entirely new phenomena; the novelty is primarily in the rigor and generality of the theoretical treatment rather than in the qualitative discovery itself.

The perplexity parameter's role is only partially explored theoretically (e.g., Theorem 7 is proven specifically for ρ=1), leaving open how tightly the theoretical guarantees connect to the range of perplexities used in practice, though this is partially addressed via experiments.
